2026-11-22-the-third-knock.title: The Third Knock
2026-11-22-the-third-knock.description: A caretaker spends the winter alone in a shuttered seaside hotel, with one instruction. If anyone knocks on the door of room fourteen from the inside, don't answer.
2026-11-22-the-third-knock.html:
The Third Knock

The Hotel Marisol closed for the winter every year on the first of November, and every year someone had to stay behind to keep the pipes from freezing. That winter, it was me.

The owner, a tired woman named Mrs. Edda Vane, gave me the keys on the last afternoon of October. She walked me through the boiler room, the fuse box, the list of numbers to call if the roof began to leak. Then, at the front door, with her coat already buttoned, she stopped.

"Room fourteen," she said. "If anyone knocks on it, don't answer."

I laughed, because I thought it was a joke about the guests. The rooms were empty. The beds were stripped. I said so.

Mrs. Vane looked at me for a long moment. "Not on the door from the corridor," she said. "From the inside."

Then she left, and the sea took the sound of her car away.

The first weeks were easy. I read. I walked the beach in the grey mornings and checked the radiators in the afternoons. The hotel settled into its winter noises: the long sigh of the boiler, the tick of cooling pipes, the wind feeling along the windows for a way in.

Room fourteen was at the far end of the second floor, where the corridor bent toward the sea. I passed it twice a day. It was an ordinary door, painted the same tired cream as all the others, with a brass number that had gone dark at the edges.

On the twentieth night, I was sitting in the porter's office, half asleep over a book, when I heard it.

Three knocks. Unhurried. Polite, almost. They came from above me, from the second floor, from the end of the corridor where it bent toward the sea.

I told myself it was the pipes. I told myself that all the way up the stairs, and all the way down the corridor, with the torch shaking a little in my hand. The door of room fourteen was closed. The corridor was empty. The air smelled of salt and old carpet.

I stood there for a long time. Nothing happened. I went back down.

It came again three nights later, and then every second night, always just after two in the morning. Always three knocks. Always from the inside of the door.

I did what Mrs. Vane had told me. I did not answer. But I began to listen. And as I listened, I noticed something I wished I had not.

The knocks were getting closer together. At first there had been a long breath between each one, the way you knock on a door when you expect to wait. By the second week, the gaps had shortened. By the third, they came quickly, one after another, like someone who has been waiting a very long time and has begun to understand that no one is coming.

On the last night of November, I went up with the torch and stood outside the door, and I spoke to it. I don't know why. Loneliness, perhaps. Or pity.

"I'm not allowed to open it," I said.

The silence on the other side changed. I can't explain it better than that. It became the silence of someone listening.

Then, very softly, from just behind the wood, a voice I almost recognised said, "That's all right. I'm not knocking to come out."

I didn't understand, and then I did. I turned and looked back down the long corridor, toward the stairs, toward the porter's office and the lamp I had left burning.

The knocking was coming from down there now. From my office. From the inside of my door.

I have not gone back down. I am still standing in the corridor of the second floor, where it bends toward the sea, and the door of room fourteen is warm against my back. Mrs. Vane comes back in March. I hope she remembers to knock.

2026-11-22-the-unison.title: The Unison
2026-11-22-the-unison.description: A piano tuner is called to a farmhouse on the moor, where one note has refused to be tuned since the owner's husband died. He has never met a string he couldn't bring into line. Until now.
2026-11-22-the-unison.html:
The Unison

I have tuned pianos for thirty-one years, and in all that time I have only ever had one complaint about my work. I want to say that at the start, so that you understand I am not a nervous man, or a careless one. When a client tells me a piano sounds wrong, I believe them. When I tell a client a piano is right, it is.

The letter came in the second week of October. It was handwritten, on thick cream paper that had gone soft at the folds, and it had been addressed to my old shop on Mill Street, which closed nine years ago. Someone at the post office had crossed out the address and written my home address underneath in blue biro. I remember thinking that was kind of them.

The letter was short. It said that the writer, a Mrs. Agnes Harrow of Hollin End Farm, owned an upright piano that had belonged to her late husband. It said the piano had not been tuned since he died, two years before. It said she had found my name on a card inside the lid, in his handwriting, with the word "reliable" underlined twice. And then, at the bottom, after her signature, there was one more line, written smaller, as if she had added it later and was not sure she should.

It said: "I would be grateful if you could come soon. I think it has begun to tune itself."

I read that line several times. Pianos do not tune themselves. They go flat, mostly, as the strings relax and the wood breathes in and out with the seasons. Left alone for two years, an old upright in a farmhouse would be a quarter tone down at least, and sour in the treble. I assumed she meant that it sounded strange to her, and that she did not have the words for it. People often don't. I wrote back and offered her the following Thursday.

Hollin End is the last farm on the road over the moor, past the reservoir, where the stone walls give up and the land turns to heather and bog cotton. It took me an hour and a half from town. The road narrowed to a single lane, then to a track with grass down the middle, and the last mile I drove at walking pace with the wipers going, though it wasn't raining. The cloud had simply come down to meet the ground.

The house was long and low and built of dark stone, with a slate roof that had sagged a little in the middle, like an old horse. There was a light in one window. When I turned off the engine, the silence was so complete that I could hear the engine ticking as it cooled, and beyond that, faintly, the wind moving across the moor. It made a sound I have since tried many times to describe. The nearest I can come is this. It sounded like someone a long way off, holding one note, and not needing to breathe.

Mrs. Harrow was in her seventies, small and straight-backed, in a grey cardigan with the sleeves pushed up. She had a farmer's hands, broad and scarred across the knuckles, and pale eyes that did not blink as often as most people's. She shook my hand firmly and thanked me for coming so far.

"Tobias always said you were the only one worth having," she said. "He said you could hear a string go out across a room."

I said that was generous of him. I did not remember her husband. I have had a great many clients. But I did not say that.

The piano was in the front room, against the inside wall, away from the damp. It was an old German upright, black, with brass candle-holders still fixed to the front panel and a crack in the veneer above the keyboard that someone had filled with wax. The room was cold and very clean. There was a range at the far end, with a kettle on it, and a single armchair turned to face the piano, not the window or the fire. I noticed that. I thought perhaps it had been his chair.

I lifted the lid and took the front panel off, and I played a scale, and then a few chords, the way I always do, to hear what I am dealing with before I touch a single pin.

It was flat, as I had expected. About a third of a semitone down across the middle, worse in the treble, a little sour in the tenor where the strings had settled unevenly. A perfectly ordinary neglected piano. I was already planning the pitch raise in my head when I reached the F sharp below middle C, and stopped.

Most notes on a piano have three strings, tuned to sound together as one. We call that a unison. When the three strings are even slightly apart, you hear beats, a soft wavering in the tone, like a voice with a tremble in it. After two years of neglect, almost every unison on that piano was beating. Some slowly, some fast. That is normal. That is what I am paid to fix.

The F sharp did not beat at all.

I played it again, and held it, and listened to it die away. Three strings, in perfect unison. Cleaner than I could have tuned them myself on my best day. And it was not an F sharp. It sat somewhere between F and F sharp, in the crack between two notes, a pitch that does not exist on any keyboard. And yet when I played it, it did not sound out of tune. It sounded like the only note on the piano that was in tune. Everything else sounded wrong around it.

"That's the one," said Mrs. Harrow. She was standing in the doorway with her arms folded. "Tobias never touched that one."

I told her I would bring it into line with the others, and she did not answer.

I worked for three hours. I brought the whole piano up to pitch, to A at four hundred and forty, the way it is supposed to be, with my tuning lever and my felt mutes and my old steel fork, which I have carried since I was an apprentice. The pins were tight in the block, which surprised me in a piano that age. The strings were sound. It was, under the neglect, a good instrument, and I enjoyed bringing it back.

I left the F sharp until last.

I set the mutes so that only one of its three strings could sound, and I put my lever on the pin, and I turned it the smallest amount. The pitch rose. I listened, and turned again, and brought it up to a true F sharp, and the string held there, singing quietly, perfectly in tune with the rest of the piano.

Then I took my hand off the lever.

The pitch slid down. Not quickly, the way it does when a pin slips in a worn block. Slowly. Smoothly. The way a weight on a rope comes down when you let the rope run through your hands. It slid down to the place between F and F sharp, and stopped there, and stayed.

I checked the pin. It was as tight as any on the piano. I tried again, and again it held while my hand was on the lever, and again it slid when I let go. The third time, I held the lever for a full minute before releasing it, and the third time it slid home all the same, as if the string had simply been waiting for me to finish.

I am not a superstitious man. I told myself that there was a fault in the bridge, a hairline crack I couldn't see, that let the string creep. I told Mrs. Harrow that I would need to order a new set of strings for that note, and come back. She nodded as if she had expected nothing else.

She made tea while I packed up my tools. I heard the kettle on the range begin to sing as it came to the boil, rising, rising. And then it settled, and held one long steady note.

I knew what note it was before I let myself think about it.

"He used to sit there for hours," Mrs. Harrow said, behind me. I turned. She was looking at the armchair. "In the evenings. Not playing. Just listening. He said the house was nearly in tune. He said it only needed a little help." She poured the tea. "I thought he was going strange, at the end. But I've been listening, since. And I think he was right."

I drank the tea standing up, and I drove home with the radio on, loudly, all the way.

The strings arrived from the supplier in ten days, and I went back up to Hollin End at the beginning of November. The bracken had gone the colour of rust, and the reservoir was low, and there were patches of old snow lying in the hollows on the high ground, grey and hard as stone.

Mrs. Harrow looked well. Better than she had. There was colour in her face, and she moved more easily, and she said she had been sleeping right through the night for the first time in years. She said it with a kind of shyness, as if it were something she had been given and did not quite deserve.

I sat down at the piano, and played a scale, and took my hands off the keys.

The whole instrument had moved.

Not flat. Not sour. Moved. Every note I had brought up to pitch ten days before had shifted, some up, some down, by amounts too small for anyone but a tuner to notice. And they had not shifted at random. They had arranged themselves. When I played a chord, it rang. When I played a scale, it was a scale. But it was not a scale that belonged to any key I knew. Every interval was a hair wider or narrower than it should have been, and all of them had been chosen, the way you might choose where to stand in a room so that you are exactly the right distance from everyone in it.

At the centre of it, holding it all together, was the F sharp that was not an F sharp.

I have tuned a great many pianos. I have never heard one that was so perfectly in tune with itself. I sat there with my hands in my lap and I was, for a moment, almost moved to tears by it. And then I was afraid. The two feelings arrived so close together that I could not tell where one ended and the other began.

I fitted the new strings. I want you to know that I did it properly. I removed the old ones, and cleaned the pins, and threaded the new wire, and brought it up slowly over the best part of an hour so as not to shock it. New wire stretches. It takes days to settle. It should have dropped a little, and gone on dropping, for a week.

It came up to the place between F and F sharp and stopped there, as if it already knew the way.

I sat back from the piano. Through the window, the cloud was coming down off the moor again, and I could hear the wind rising in the chimney. It made a low, steady sound in the flue. In the kitchen, the old refrigerator was humming. Somewhere a tap was dripping into a steel sink, a small bright tick, again and again. And all of those sounds, every one, sat on the same note, or on a note that belonged with it, so that the whole house, standing there on the moor in the failing light, was sounding one long, quiet chord.

The piano was not out of tune with the house. The piano had been the last thing in the house that was.

"You don't have to fight it," Mrs. Harrow said. She was in the doorway again. I had not heard her come. "Tobias fought it for years. He didn't understand at first. None of us did." She smiled at me then, a kind, tired smile. "But you can hear it. He said you would. That's why he kept your card."

I asked her what she meant. I asked her what it was. I remember my voice sounded strange to me, thin and harsh, like a string with a fault in it.

She thought about it for a long time before she answered.

"It's the note the house makes," she said. "When everything in it agrees."

I did not take her money. I put my tools in the car without packing them properly and I drove down off the moor with the window open and the cold air roaring in, because I did not want to hear anything at all.

I should tell you about the next three weeks, though I am not proud of them.

The first thing I noticed was the fork. My tuning fork is a plain steel fork, stamped with the letter A and the number four hundred and forty. Steel forks do not change. That is the point of them. I have trusted that fork for thirty-one years.

On the Monday after I came down from Hollin End, I struck it on my knee in a client's sitting room, and held it to my ear, and it was wrong.

Not by much. A hair. But wrong. I checked it against the electronic tuner I keep in my bag for clients who like to see a needle. The needle sat at four hundred and forty, exactly, steady as a stone. I struck the fork again. Wrong. The needle said one thing and my ear said another, and for the first time in my working life I did not know which of them to believe.

I tuned that piano by the needle. When I played it afterwards, every chord made my teeth ache. The client, a retired schoolteacher, said it sounded lovely. I thanked her and left and sat in my car for twenty minutes with my hands on the wheel.

It got worse. Or perhaps I mean it got clearer. I began to hear the note everywhere. Not loudly. Underneath things. In the hum of the strip lights at the supermarket. In the bus idling at the lights on Mill Street. In my own refrigerator, at three in the morning, when I lay awake and listened to it and knew, the way you know when someone is standing behind you, that it had begun to settle. That it was being pulled, very slowly, the way the string had been pulled when I took my hand off the lever.

And everything that was not on the note sounded worse and worse. My clients' pianos. The radio. Music I had loved since I was a boy. All of it began to sound to me like a room full of people talking at once, each of them slightly wrong, none of them listening to the others. I had spent my whole life listening to beats, those small tremblings where two notes almost agree and do not quite. I had spent my whole life fixing them. Now I could hear nothing else. The whole world was beating, like a sick pulse, all the time.

I started to hum it. I did not decide to. I would find myself in the kitchen or the car, humming one low note, and it would take me a moment to understand that the sound was coming from me. And when I stopped, the silence felt thin and sour, and I wanted to start again.

That was when I had my complaint. A man in the new houses by the ring road, who rang me the day after I tuned his daughter's piano and said, quite politely, that it sounded like something was wrong with it. That every note sounded as if it were leaning towards something. He said his daughter had cried when she played it. I apologised and went back and tuned it again, by the needle, and I did not let myself listen.

On the last day of November, a second letter came. Thick cream paper, soft at the folds. It said only this.

"It is nearly finished. There is only one voice still out. I think you know which one. Come when you are ready. Agnes."

I went up in the first week of December. There had been snow on the high ground, and the track to Hollin End was white between the dark walls, and the reservoir lay black and still, without a ripple on it.

I had brought wire cutters. I want to be honest about that. I had told myself, all the way up the valley, that I was going to cut that string out of the piano, and the two beside it, and nail the hammer down if I had to, and that whatever was happening to me would stop. I believed it until I turned off the engine.

The silence came down, and the wind was moving over the moor, and it was holding one note.

The front door was open. Mrs. Harrow was in the armchair, facing the piano, with her hands folded in her lap and her eyes closed. She was breathing slowly. She did not look up when I came in. She was not asleep. Her lips were very slightly parted, and she was humming, so softly that I could barely hear it, one low note.

The piano lid was open.

I walked across the room and put my hand on the case, and I felt it through the wood. The whole instrument was sounding, very quietly, though no one was touching the keys. The wind in the chimney. The kettle on the range, though the fire was out and the kettle was cold. The windows in their frames. The slates on the roof. The stone walls themselves. All of it was holding one chord, the way a church holds the last chord of the organ after the organist has lifted his hands. And at the centre of it, holding it all, was the F sharp that was not an F sharp.

I took out the wire cutters, and I set the jaws around the first of the three strings, and I listened, the way I have listened for thirty-one years, to find exactly where the sound was coming from.

It was not coming from the string.

It had never been coming from the string. The string was only answering. The sound was coming from the walls, and the roof, and the cold kettle, and the old woman in the armchair, and from under the floor, from the stone and the peat and the black water of the reservoir and the long dark moor beyond it, all of it agreeing, all of it in tune.

And it was coming from me.

I was humming. I do not know how long I had been humming. I was standing at the piano with the wire cutters in my hand and my mouth half open, holding one note, and the note was exactly right. For the first time in my life there were no beats. Not one. The trembling that I had been listening to since I was a boy, in every piano and every voice and every room I had ever stood in, was gone, and in its place there was only this one clear, enormous, patient sound, and I was part of it, and it was not sour, and it was not wrong, and it did not need anything else from me ever again.

I did not cut the string.

I am writing this at the kitchen table at Hollin End. Agnes says someone from the village will post it for me. The snow has closed the road, and I do not mind. In the evenings we sit in the front room, she in the armchair and I on the piano stool, and we do not play. We listen. When the wind comes up off the reservoir, the whole house sounds, and so do we.

I have left my card inside the lid. My handwriting. The word "reliable", underlined twice.

If you are a tuner, and you have a good ear, and one day you get a letter in thick cream paper from the last farm on the road over the moor, I would not come. Unless you are tired. Unless you have spent your whole life listening to the world beat and tremble and fail to agree, and you have begun to wonder, as I did, what it would be like to hear it stop.

2026-11-22-the-temple.title: The Temple, by H. P. Lovecraft
2026-11-22-the-temple.description: A classic of weird fiction from 1925. A German submarine commander in the First World War writes his last testament from the ocean floor, after a carved ivory head taken from a drowned sailor leads his crew, one by one, into madness, and his crippled U-boat drifts down onto a sunken city.
2026-11-22-the-temple.html:
The Temple

By H. P. Lovecraft. First published in Weird Tales, in nineteen twenty-five.

On August 20, 1917, I, Karl Heinrich, Graf von Altberg-Ehrenstein, Lieutenant-Commander in the Imperial German Navy and in charge of the submarine U-29, deposit this bottle and record in the Atlantic Ocean at a point to me unknown but probably about North Latitude 20 degrees, West Longitude 35 degrees, where my ship lies disabled on the ocean floor. I do so because of my desire to set certain unusual facts before the public; a thing I shall not in all probability survive to accomplish in person, since the circumstances surrounding me are as menacing as they are extraordinary, and involve not only the hopeless crippling of the U-29, but the impairment of my iron German will in a manner most disastrous.

On the afternoon of June 18, as reported by wireless to the U-61, bound for Kiel, we torpedoed the British freighter Victory, New York to Liverpool, in North Latitude 45 degrees 16 minutes, West Longitude 28 degrees 34 minutes; permitting the crew to leave in boats in order to obtain a good cinema view for the admiralty records. The ship sank quite picturesquely, bow first, the stern rising high out of the water whilst the hull shot down perpendicularly to the bottom of the sea. Our camera missed nothing, and I regret that so fine a reel of film should never reach Berlin. After that we sank the lifeboats with our guns and submerged.

When we rose to the surface about sunset, a seaman's body was found on the deck, hands gripping the railing in curious fashion. The poor fellow was young, rather dark, and very handsome; probably an Italian or Greek, and undoubtedly of the Victory's crew. He had evidently sought refuge on the very ship which had been forced to destroy his own—one more victim of the unjust war of aggression which the English pig-dogs are waging upon the Fatherland. Our men searched him for souvenirs, and found in his coat pocket a very odd bit of ivory carved to represent a youth's head crowned with laurel. My fellow-officer, Lieutenant Klenze, believed that the thing was of great age and artistic value, so took it from the men for himself. How it had ever come into the possession of a common sailor neither he nor I could imagine.

As the dead man was thrown overboard there occurred two incidents which created much disturbance amongst the crew. The fellow's eyes had been closed; but in the dragging of his body to the rail they were jarred open, and many seemed to entertain a queer delusion that they gazed steadily and mockingly at Schmidt and Zimmer, who were bent over the corpse. The Boatswain Muller, an elderly man who would have known better had he not been a superstitious Alsatian swine, became so excited by this impression that he watched the body in the water; and swore that after it sank a little it drew its limbs into a swimming position and sped away to the south under the waves. Klenze and I did not like these displays of peasant ignorance, and severely reprimanded the men, particularly Muller.

The next day a very troublesome situation was created by the indisposition of some of the crew. They were evidently suffering from the nervous strain of our long voyage, and had had bad dreams. Several seemed quite dazed and stupid; and after satisfying myself that they were not feigning their weakness, I excused them from their duties. The sea was rather rough, so we descended to a depth where the waves were less troublesome. Here we were comparatively calm, despite a somewhat puzzling southward current which we could not identify from our oceanographic charts. The moans of the sick men were decidedly annoying; but since they did not appear to demoralize the rest of the crew, we did not resort to extreme measures. It was our plan to remain where we were and intercept the liner Dacia, mentioned in information from agents in New York.

In the early evening we rose to the surface, and found the sea less heavy. The smoke of a battleship was on the northern horizon, but our distance and ability to submerge made us safe. What worried us more was the talk of Boatswain Muller, which grew wilder as night came on. He was in a detestably childish state, and babbled of some illusion of dead bodies drifting past the undersea portholes; bodies which looked at him intensely, and which he recognized in spite of bloating as having seen dying during some of our victorious German exploits. And he said that the young man we had found and tossed overboard was their leader. This was very gruesome and abnormal, so we confined Muller in irons and had him soundly whipped. The men were not pleased at his punishment, but discipline was necessary. We also denied the request of a delegation headed by Seaman Zimmer, that the curious carved ivory head be cast into the sea.

On June 20, Seaman Bohm and Schmidt, who had been ill the day before, became violently insane. I regretted that no physician was included in our complement of officers, since German lives are precious; but the constant ravings of the two concerning a terrible curse were most subversive of discipline, so drastic steps were taken. The crew accepted the event in a sullen fashion, but it seemed to quiet Muller; who thereafter gave us no trouble. In the evening we released him, and he went about his duties silently.

In the week that followed we were all very nervous, watching for the Dacia. The tension was aggravated by the disappearance of Muller and Zimmer, who undoubtedly committed suicide as a result of the fears which had seemed to harass them, though they were not observed in the act of jumping overboard. I was rather glad to be rid of Muller, for even his silence had unfavorably affected the crew. Everyone seemed inclined to be silent now, as though holding a secret fear. Many were ill, but none made a disturbance. Lieutenant Klenze chafed under the strain, and was annoyed by the merest trifle—such as the school of dolphins which gathered about the U-29 in increasing numbers, and the growing intensity of that southward current which was not on our chart.

It at length became apparent that we had missed the Dacia altogether. Such failures are not uncommon, and we were more pleased than disappointed, since our return to Wilhelmshaven was now in order. At noon June 28 we turned northeastward, and despite some rather comical entanglements with the unusual masses of dolphins, were soon under way.

The explosion in the engine room at 2 A.M. was wholly a surprise. No defect in the machinery or carelessness in the men had been noticed, yet without warning the ship was racked from end to end with a colossal shock. Lieutenant Klenze hurried to the engine room, finding the fuel-tank and most of the mechanism shattered, and Engineers Raabe and Schneider instantly killed. Our situation had suddenly become grave indeed; for though the chemical air regenerators were intact, and though we could use the devices for raising and submerging the ship and opening the hatches as long as compressed air and storage batteries might hold out, we were powerless to propel or guide the submarine. To seek rescue in the life-boats would be to deliver ourselves into the hands of enemies unreasonably embittered against our great German nation, and our wireless had failed ever since the Victory affair to put us in touch with a fellow U-boat of the Imperial Navy.

From the hour of the accident till July 2 we drifted constantly to the south, almost without plans and encountering no vessel. Dolphins still encircled the U-29, a somewhat remarkable circumstance considering the distance we had covered. On the morning of July 2 we sighted a warship flying American colors, and the men became very restless in their desire to surrender. Finally Lieutenant Menze had to shoot a seaman named Traube, who urged this un-German act with especial violence. This quieted the crew for the time, and we submerged unseen.

The next afternoon a dense flock of sea-birds appeared from the south, and the ocean began to heave ominously. Closing our hatches, we awaited developments until we realized that we must either submerge or be swamped in the mounting waves. Our air pressure and electricity were diminishing, and we wished to avoid all unnecessary use of our slender mechanical resources; but in this case there was no choice. We did not descend far, and when after several hours the sea was calmer, we decided to return to the surface. Here, however, a new trouble developed; for the ship failed to respond to our direction in spite of all that the mechanics could do. As the men grew more frightened at this undersea imprisonment, some of them began to mutter again about Lieutenant Klenze's ivory image, but the sight of an automatic pistol calmed them. We kept the poor devils as busy as we could, tinkering at the machinery even when we knew it was useless.

Klenze and I usually slept at different times; and it was during my sleep, about 5 A.M., July 4, that the general mutiny broke loose. The six remaining pigs of seamen, suspecting that we were lost, had suddenly burst into a mad fury at our refusal to surrender to the Yankee battleship two days before, and were in a delirium of cursing and destruction. They roared like the animals they were, and broke instruments and furniture indiscriminately; screaming about such nonsense as the curse of the ivory image and the dark dead youth who looked at them and swam away. Lieutenant Klenze seemed paralyzed and inefficient, as one might expect of a soft, womanish Rhinelander. I shot all six men, for it was necessary, and made sure that none remained alive.

We expelled the bodies through the double hatches and were alone in the U-29. Klenze seemed very nervous, and drank heavily. It was decided that we remain alive as long as possible, using the large stock of provisions and chemical supply of oxygen, none of which had suffered from the crazy antics of those swine-hound seamen. Our compasses, depth gauges, and other delicate instruments were ruined; so that henceforth our only reckoning would be guess work, based on our watches, the calendar, and our apparent drift as judged by any objects we might spy through the portholes or from the conning tower. Fortunately we had storage batteries still capable of long use, both for interior lighting and for the searchlight. We often cast a beam around the ship, but saw only dolphins, swimming parallel to our own drifting course. I was scientifically interested in those dolphins; for though the ordinary Delphinus delphis is a cetacean mammal, unable to subsist without air, I watched one of the swimmers closely for two hours, and did not see him alter his submerged condition.

With the passage of time Klenze and I decided that we were still drifting south, meanwhile sinking deeper and deeper. We noted the marine fauna and flora, and read much on the subject in the books I had carried with me for spare moments. I could not help observing, however, the inferior scientific knowledge of my companion. His mind was not Prussian, but given to imaginings and speculations which have no value. The fact of our coming death affected him curiously, and he would frequently pray in remorse over the men, women, and children we had sent to the bottom; forgetting that all things are noble which serve the German state. After a time he became noticeably unbalanced, gazing for hours at his ivory image and weaving fanciful stories of the lost and forgotten things under the sea. Sometimes, as a psychological experiment, I would lead him on in the wanderings, and listen to his endless poetical quotations and tales of sunken ships. I was very sorry for him, for I dislike to see a German suffer; but he was not a good man to die with. For myself I was proud, knowing how the Fatherland would revere my memory and how my sons would be taught to be men like me.

On August 9, we espied the ocean floor, and sent a powerful beam from the searchlight over it. It was a vast undulating plain, mostly covered with seaweed, and strewn with the shells of small mollusks. Here and there were slimy objects of puzzling contour, draped with weeds and encrusted with barnacles, which Klenze declared must be ancient ships lying in their graves. He was puzzled by one thing, a peak of solid matter, protruding above the oceanbed nearly four feet at its apex; about two feet thick, with flat sides and smooth upper surfaces which met at a very obtuse angle. I called the peak a bit of outcropping rock, but Klenze thought he saw carvings on it. After a while he began to shudder, and turned away from the scene as if frightened; yet could give no explanation save that he was overcome with the vastness, darkness, remoteness, antiquity, and mystery of the oceanic abysses. His mind was tired, but I am always a German, and was quick to notice two things: that the U-29 was standing the deep-sea pressure splendidly, and that the peculiar dolphins were still about us, even at a depth where the existence of high organisms is considered impossible by most naturalists. That I had previously overestimated our depth, I was sure; but none the less we must still have been deep enough to make these phenomena remarkable. Our southward speed, as gauged by the ocean floor, was about as I had estimated from the organisms passed at higher levels.

It was at three fifteen P.M., August 12, that poor Klenze went wholly mad. He had been in the conning tower using the searchlight when I saw him bound into the library compartment where I sat reading, and his face at once betrayed him. I will repeat here what he said, underlining the words he emphasized: "He is calling! He is calling! I hear him! We must go!" As he spoke he took his ivory image from the table, pocketed it, and seized my arm in an effort to drag me up the companionway to the deck. In a moment I understood that he meant to open the hatch and plunge with me into the water outside, a vagary of suicidal and homicidal mania for which I was scarcely prepared. As I hung back and attempted to soothe him he grew more violent, saying: "Come now—do not wait until later; it is better to repent and be forgiven than to defy and be condemned." Then I tried the opposite of the soothing plan, and told him he was mad—pitifully demented. But he was unmoved, and cried: "If I am mad, it is mercy. May the gods pity the man who in his callousness can remain sane to the hideous end! Come and be mad whilst he still calls with mercy!"

This outburst seemed to relieve a pressure in his brain; for as he finished he grew much milder, asking me to let him depart alone if I would not accompany him. My course at once became clear. He was a German, but only a Rhinelander and a commoner; and he was now a potentially dangerous madman. By complying with his suicidal request I could immediately free myself from one who was no longer a companion but a menace. I asked him to give me the ivory image before he went, but this request brought from him such uncanny laughter that I did not repeat it. Then I asked him if he wished to leave any keepsake or lock of hair for his family in Germany in case I should be rescued, but again he gave me that strange laugh. So as he climbed the ladder I went to the levers and, allowing proper time-intervals, operated the machinery which sent him to his death. After I saw that he was no longer in the boat I threw the searchlight around the water in an effort to obtain a last glimpse of him since I wished to ascertain whether the water-pressure would flatten him as it theoretically should, or whether the body would be unaffected, like those extraordinary dolphins. I did not, however, succeed in finding my late companion, for the dolphins were massed thickly and obscuringly about the conning tower.

That evening I regretted that I had not taken the ivory image surreptitiously from poor Klenze's pocket as he left, for the memory of it fascinated me. I could not forget the youthful, beautiful head with its leafy crown, though I am not by nature an artist. I was also sorry that I had no one with whom to converse. Klenze, though not my mental equal, was much better than no one. I did not sleep well that night, and wondered exactly when the end would come. Surely, I had little enough chance of rescue.

The next day I ascended to the conning tower and commenced the customary searchlight explorations. Northward the view was much the same as it had been all the four days since we had sighted the bottom, but I perceived that the drifting of the U-29 was less rapid. As I swung the beam around to the south, I noticed that the ocean floor ahead fell away in a marked declivity, and bore curiously regular blocks of stone in certain places, disposed as if in accordance with definite patterns. The boat did not at once descend to match the greater ocean depth, so I was soon forced to adjust the searchlight to cast a sharply downward beam. Owing to the abruptness of the change a wire was disconnected, which necessitated a delay of many minutes for repairs; but at length the light streamed on again, flooding the marine valley below me.

I am not given to emotion of any kind, but my amazement was very great when I saw what lay revealed in that electrical glow. And yet as one reared in the best Kultur of Prussia, I should not have been amazed, for geology and tradition alike tell us of great transpositions in oceanic and continental areas. What I saw was an extended and elaborate array of ruined edifices; all of magnificent though unclassified architecture, and in various stages of preservation. Most appeared to be of marble, gleaming whitely in the rays of the searchlight, and the general plan was of a large city at the bottom of a narrow valley, with numerous isolated temples and villas on the steep slopes above. Roofs were fallen and columns were broken, but there still remained an air of immemorially ancient splendor which nothing could efface.

Confronted at last with the Atlantis I had formerly deemed largely a myth, I was the most eager of explorers. At the bottom of that valley a river once had flowed; for as I examined the scene more closely I beheld the remains of stone and marble bridges and sea-walls, and terraces and embankments once verdant and beautiful. In my enthusiasm I became nearly as idiotic and sentimental as poor Klenze, and was very tardy in noticing that the southward current had ceased at last, allowing the U-29 to settle slowly down upon the sunken city as an airplane settles upon a town of the upper earth. I was slow, too, in realizing that the school of unusual dolphins had vanished.

In about two hours the boat rested in a paved plaza close to the rocky wall of the valley. On one side I could view the entire city as it sloped from the plaza down to the old river-bank; on the other side, in startling proximity, I was confronted by the richly ornate and perfectly preserved facade of a great building, evidently a temple, hollowed from the solid rock. Of the original workmanship of this titanic thing I can only make conjectures. The facade, of immense magnitude, apparently covers a continuous hollow recess; for its windows are many and widely distributed. In the center yawns a great open door, reached by an impressive flight of steps, and surrounded by exquisite carvings like the figures of Bacchanals in relief. Foremost of all are the great columns and frieze, both decorated with sculptures of inexpressible beauty; obviously portraying idealized pastoral scenes and processions of priests and priestesses bearing strange ceremonial devices in adoration of a radiant god. The art is of the most phenomenal perfection, largely Hellenic in idea, yet strangely individual. It imparts an impression of terrible antiquity, as though it were the remotest rather than the immediate ancestor of Greek art. Nor can I doubt that every detail of this massive product was fashioned from the virgin hillside rock of our planet. It is palpably a part of the valley wall, though how the vast interior was ever excavated I cannot imagine. Perhaps a cavern or series of caverns furnished the nucleus. Neither age nor submersion has corroded the pristine grandeur of this awful fane—for fane indeed it must be—and today after thousands of years it rests untarnished and inviolate in the endless night and silence of an ocean-chasm.

I cannot reckon the number of hours I spent in gazing at the sunken city with its buildings, arches, statues, and bridges, and the colossal temple with its beauty and mystery. Though I knew that death was near, my curiosity was consuming; and I threw the searchlight beam about in eager quest. The shaft of light permitted me to learn many details, but refused to show anything within the gaping door of the rock-hewn temple; and after a time I turned off the current, conscious of the need of conserving power. The rays were now perceptibly dimmer than they had been during the weeks of drifting. And as if sharpened by the coming deprivation of light, my desire to explore the watery secrets grew. I, a German, should be the first to tread those eon-forgotten ways!

I produced and examined a deep-sea diving suit of jointed metal, and experimented with the portable light and air regenerator. Though I should have trouble in managing the double hatches alone, I believed I could overcome all obstacles with my scientific skill and actually walk about the dead city in person.

On August 16 I effected an exit from the U-29, and laboriously made my way through the ruined and mud-choked streets to the ancient river. I found no skeletons or other human remains, but gleaned a wealth of archeological lore from sculptures and coins. Of this I cannot now speak save to utter my awe at a culture in the full noon of glory when cave-dwellers roamed Europe and the Nile flowed unwatched to the sea. Others, guided by this manuscript if it shall ever be found, must unfold the mysteries at which I can only hint. I returned to the boat as my electric batteries grew feeble, resolved to explore the rock temple on the following day.

On the 17th, as my impulse to search out the mystery of the temple waxed still more insistent, a great disappointment befell me; for I found that the materials needed to replenish the portable light had perished in the mutiny of those pigs in July. My rage was unbounded, yet my German sense forbade me to venture unprepared into an utterly black interior which might prove the lair of some indescribable marine monster or a labyrinth of passages from whose windings I could never extricate myself. All I could do was to turn on the waning searchlight of the U-29, and with its aid walk up the temple steps and study the exterior carvings. The shaft of light entered the door at an upward angle, and I peered in to see if I could glimpse anything, but all in vain. Not even the roof was visible; and though I took a step or two inside after testing the floor with a staff, I dared not go farther. Moreover, for the first time in my life I experienced the emotion of dread. I began to realize how some of poor Klenze's moods had arisen, for as the temple drew me more and more, I feared its aqueous abysses with a blind and mounting terror. Returning to the submarine, I turned off the lights and sat thinking in the dark. Electricity must now be saved for emergencies.

Saturday the 18th I spent in total darkness, tormented by thoughts and memories that threatened to overcome my German will. Klenze had gone mad and perished before reaching this sinister remnant of a past unwholesomely remote, and had advised me to go with him. Was, indeed, Fate preserving my reason only to draw me irresistibly to an end more horrible and unthinkable than any man has dreamed of? Clearly, my nerves were sorely taxed, and I must cast off these impressions of weaker men.

I could not sleep Saturday night, and turned on the lights regardless of the future. It was annoying that the electricity should not last out the air and provisions. I revived my thoughts of euthanasia, and examined my automatic pistol. Toward morning I must have dropped asleep with the lights on, for I awoke in darkness yesterday afternoon to find the batteries dead. I struck several matches in succession, and desperately regretted the improvidence which had caused us long ago to use up the few candles we carried.

After the fading of the last match I dared to waste, I sat very quietly without a light. As I considered the inevitable end my mind ran over preceding events, and developed a hitherto dormant impression which would have caused a weaker and more superstitious man to shudder. The head of the radiant god in the sculptures on the rock temple is the same as that carven bit of ivory which the dead sailor brought from the sea and which poor Klenze carried back into the sea.

I was a little dazed by this coincidence, but did not become terrified. It is only the inferior thinker who hastens to explain the singular and the complex by the primitive shortcut of supernaturalism. The coincidence was strange, but I was too sound a reasoner to connect circumstances which admit of no logical connection, or to associate in any uncanny fashion the disastrous events which had led from the Victory affair to my present plight. Feeling the need of more rest, I took a sedative and secured some more sleep. My nervous condition was reflected in my dreams, for I seemed to hear the cries of drowning persons, and to see dead faces pressing against the portholes of the boat. And among the dead faces was the living, mocking face of the youth with the ivory image.

I must be careful how I record my awakening today, for I am unstrung, and much hallucination is necessarily mixed with fact. Psychologically my case is most interesting, and I regret that it cannot be observed scientifically by a competent German authority. Upon opening my eyes my first sensation was an overmastering desire to visit the rock temple; a desire which grew every instant, yet which I automatically sought to resist through some emotion of fear which operated in the reverse direction. Next there came to me the impression of light amidst the darkness of dead batteries, and I seemed to see a sort of phosphorescent glow in the water through the porthole which opened toward the temple. This aroused my curiosity, for I knew of no deep-sea organism capable of emitting such luminosity.

But before I could investigate there came a third impression which because of its irrationality caused me to doubt the objectivity of anything my senses might record. It was an aural delusion; a sensation of rhythmic, melodic sound as of some wild yet beautiful chant or choral hymn, coming from the outside through the absolutely sound-proof hull of the U-29. Convinced of my psychological and nervous abnormallty, I lighted some matches and poured a stiff dose of sodium bromide solution, which seemed to calm me to the extent of dispelling the illusion of sound. But the phosphorescence remained, and I had difficulty in repressing a childish impulse to go to the porthole and seek its source. It was horribly realistic, and I could soon distinguish by its aid the familiar objects around me, as well as the empty sodium bromide glass of which I had had no former visual impression in its present location. This last circumstance made me ponder, and I crossed the room and touched the glass. It was indeed in the place where I had seemed to see it. Now I knew that the light was either real or part of an hallucination so fixed and consistent that I could not hope to dispel it, so abandoning all resistance I ascended to the conning tower to look for the luminous agency. Might it not actually be another U-boat, offering possibilities of rescue?

It is well that the reader accept nothing which follows as objective truth, for since the events transcend natural law, they are necessarily the subjective and unreal creations of my overtaxed mind. When I attained the conning tower I found the sea in general far less luminous than I had expected. There was no animal or vegetable phosphorescence about, and the city that sloped down to the river was invisible in blackness. What I did see was not spectacular, not grotesque or terrifying, yet it removed my last vestige of trust in my consciousness. For the door and windows of the undersea temple hewn from the rocky hill were vividly aglow with a flickering radiance, as from a mighty altar-flame far within.

Later incidents are chaotic. As I stared at the uncannily lighted door and windows, I became subject to the most extravagant visions—visions so extravagant that I cannot even relate them. I fancied that I discerned objects in the temple; objects both stationary and moving; and seemed to hear again the unreal chant that had floated to me when first I awaked. And over all rose thoughts and fears which centered in the youth from the sea and the ivory image whose carving was duplicated on the frieze and columns of the temple before me. I thought of poor Klenze, and wondered where his body rested with the image he had carried back into the sea. He had warned me of something, and I had not heeded—but he was a soft-headed Rhinelander who went mad at troubles a Prussian could bear with ease.

The rest is very simple. My impulse to visit and enter the temple has now become an inexplicable and imperious command which ultimately cannot be denied. My own German will no longer controls my acts, and volition is henceforward possible only in minor matters. Such madness it was which drove Klenze to his death, bare-headed and unprotected in the ocean; but I am a Prussian and a man of sense, and will use to the last what little will I have. When first I saw that I must go, I prepared my diving suit, helmet, and air regenerator for instant donning, and immediately commenced to write this hurried chronicle in the hope that it may some day reach the world. I shall seal the manuscript in a bottle and entrust it to the sea as I leave the U-29 for ever.

I have no fear, not even from the prophecies of the madman Klenze. What I have seen cannot be true, and I know that this madness of my own will at most lead only to suffocation when my air is gone. The light in the temple is a sheer delusion, and I shall die calmly like a German, in the black and forgotten depths. This demoniac laughter which I hear as I write comes only from my own weakening brain. So I will carefully don my suit and walk boldly up the steps into the primal shrine, that silent secret of unfathomed waters and uncounted years.

2026-11-22-the-indifferent-cosmos.description: How a writer who died poor and nearly unknown in 1937 shaped a century of horror, from pulp magazines and role-playing games to Alien, True Detective, Bloodborne and the SCP Foundation, and how today's writers are arguing with the darkest parts of his legacy.
2026-11-22-the-indifferent-cosmos.html:
The Indifferent Cosmos

An essay on H. P. Lovecraft and modern cosmic horror.

In March of 1937, a forty-six-year-old man died in a hospital in Providence, Rhode Island. He had cancer of the small intestine, and he had known for some time that he was dying. He left behind a modest number of stories, most of them published in cheap pulp magazines, printed on paper so poor that it yellowed within a few years. He left behind tens of thousands of letters. He had almost no money. He had never published a book of his fiction with a major publisher. By most of the measures his own century cared about, he had failed.

His name was Howard Phillips Lovecraft. And today, almost ninety years later, you can buy a plush toy of his most famous monster, a squid-faced god asleep at the bottom of the Pacific, in shops all over the world. His invented town of Arkham appears in comic books, board games and video games. His imaginary book of forbidden knowledge, the Necronomicon, is so well known that people still ask librarians whether it is real. The phrase "Lovecraftian" has become an ordinary word, used by film critics, game designers and people describing a bad day at the office.

How did that happen? How did a man who died believing himself a failure become one of the most influential horror writers of all time? And why, in the twenty-first century, does his particular kind of fear feel more relevant than ever, even as writers wrestle openly with the ugliest parts of his work?

What cosmic horror actually is

Most horror, for most of its history, has been about evil. The vampire wants your blood. The ghost wants revenge. The devil wants your soul. These are terrible things, but they are also, in a strange way, comforting. They tell you that you matter. Something out there has noticed you, and wants you, and has a reason.

Lovecraft's great idea was to take that comfort away.

He called his philosophy cosmicism. The universe, as he saw it, was unimaginably vast and unimaginably old, and human beings were a brief accident on a minor planet, of no more importance to the cosmos than a colony of mould. The forces that truly ran the universe, if they could be called forces at all, did not hate us. They did not love us either. They simply did not notice us. And if they ever did notice us, it would be in the way we notice ants on a path we happen to be walking down.

In his long essay Supernatural Horror in Literature, written in the late nineteen-twenties, Lovecraft opened with a sentence that has been quoted ever since. "The oldest and strongest emotion of mankind is fear, and the oldest and strongest kind of fear is fear of the unknown."

And in The Call of Cthulhu, published in nineteen twenty-eight, he put the same idea in its most famous form. The story begins: "The most merciful thing in the world, I think, is the inability of the human mind to correlate all its contents."

That sentence is the key to everything that followed. In Lovecraft's stories, the danger is not really the monster. The danger is understanding. His narrators are scholars, scientists, antiquarians, people who go looking for knowledge. And the knowledge they find is that the world is not what they thought it was, that humanity is not the centre of anything, and that the truth is so large and so alien that the mind cannot hold it. They go mad not because something attacks them, but because they finally see.

This is why Lovecraft's monsters are so often described as indescribable. Critics have mocked him for it, for all those adjectives like unnameable and unspeakable and eldritch. But the vagueness is the point. A monster you can describe is a monster you can understand, and a monster you can understand is already less frightening. Cosmic horror is the horror of scale, of deep time and deep space, of the gap between what is out there and what a human being can comprehend.

How the mythos escaped

Lovecraft did something else that turned out to matter enormously. He shared.

He was part of a circle of writers who corresponded constantly, people like Clark Ashton Smith, Robert E. Howard, the creator of Conan, and a teenage Robert Bloch, who would later write Psycho. They borrowed each other's inventions as a kind of game. A forbidden book from one writer's story would turn up on a shelf in another's. A god mentioned in passing by one would become the centre of a tale by someone else. Long before anyone used the phrase, they were building a shared universe.

After Lovecraft's death, two of his friends, August Derleth and Donald Wandrei, founded a small publishing house called Arkham House, mostly to get his stories into proper hardback books. Its first title, in nineteen thirty-nine, was a collection of his fiction. Without Arkham House, much of Lovecraft's work might simply have crumbled away with the pulps.

Derleth also gave the shared world a name, the Cthulhu Mythos. And he changed it. Derleth was a more conventional thinker than Lovecraft, and he reshaped the mythos into something closer to a battle between good and evil, with benevolent elder gods opposing the dark ones, and neat categories of creatures tied to the classical elements. Many later fans felt this softened the very thing that made Lovecraft distinctive. In Derleth's version, the universe cared after all. But the name stuck, and so did the idea that this was a world anyone could write in.

The next great leap came in nineteen eighty-one, when a small company called Chaosium published a tabletop role-playing game called Call of Cthulhu, designed by Sandy Petersen. Most role-playing games of the time were about heroes growing stronger. Call of Cthulhu had a statistic called Sanity, and it only really went one way. The more your character learned about the truth of the universe, the closer they came to breaking. It was a brilliant translation of Lovecraft's central idea into a game mechanic, and it introduced his world to a whole generation who had never read a pulp magazine.

There is one more reason the mythos spread so far. Most of Lovecraft's work is in the public domain, and the copyright status of the rest has been murky and contested for decades. In practice, his creations became something like folklore. No studio owns Cthulhu. Anyone can write about Arkham. And so everyone did.

The shadow in the work

Any honest account of Lovecraft's legacy has to face something difficult. Lovecraft was a racist, and not in a casual way. His letters are full of contempt for immigrants, for Black people, for almost anyone who was not of the old English stock he imagined himself to belong to. And this is not separate from his fiction. In some of his stories, it is the engine.

The Horror at Red Hook, from nineteen twenty-five, was written after an unhappy period living in New York, and its fear of the city's immigrant neighbourhoods is barely disguised. The Shadow over Innsmouth, one of his most admired stories, is built around a horror of mixed ancestry, of a family line that turns out not to be what it seemed. When you read Lovecraft closely, the cosmic dread of an indifferent universe and a much more ordinary, much uglier dread of other people are often tangled together.

For a long time, the horror community mostly looked away. That changed in the twenty-tens. The World Fantasy Award, one of the most prestigious prizes in the field, had for decades been a small bust of Lovecraft's face. When the Nigerian American writer Nnedi Okorafor won it in twenty eleven, she wrote publicly about what it meant to receive an award shaped like a man who had written about people like her with such contempt. Other writers took up the argument. In twenty fifteen, the organisers announced that the bust would be retired.

What happened next is, to my mind, the most interesting chapter in Lovecraft's whole legacy. Writers did not simply reject him. They answered him.

In twenty sixteen, Victor LaValle published a novella called The Ballad of Black Tom, which retells The Horror at Red Hook from the point of view of a young Black man in Harlem, the kind of character Lovecraft's story would have treated as part of the menace. LaValle dedicated the book to Lovecraft, "with all my conflicted feelings." The same year, Matt Ruff published Lovecraft Country, which sets cosmic horror against the very real horrors of the segregated United States in the nineteen-fifties, and which became a television series in twenty twenty. Ruthanna Emrys, in her novel Winter Tide, took the fish-like people of Innsmouth, Lovecraft's great symbol of contamination, and made them the sympathetic heart of the story, a persecuted community rather than a threat. And N. K. Jemisin's The City We Became pits the living spirit of New York, in all its mixture and noise, against a cold, alien force that wants to erase it.

These books share something important. They keep the cosmic part. They keep the vastness, the indifference, the sense that reality is stranger and larger than we can grasp. What they reject is the idea that the people on the margins are the monsters. In their hands, the horror of an uncaring universe becomes something different. Sometimes the cosmos is not the only thing that is indifferent to your survival. Sometimes society is too. And the people who already know that might be better prepared for the truth than anyone in Lovecraft's libraries.

Cosmic horror on the screen

Lovecraft has always been hard to film. How do you show a monster whose whole point is that it cannot be shown? Direct adaptations have often struggled. Guillermo del Toro spent years trying to make At the Mountains of Madness as a big studio film, and the project stalled around twenty eleven, reportedly because the studio would not fund an expensive horror film with an adult rating.

But Lovecraft's influence on cinema is far larger than the list of films with his name on them.

Think of Alien, from nineteen seventy-nine. Its co-writer, Dan O'Bannon, admired Lovecraft, and its creature was designed by the Swiss artist H. R. Giger, whose book of paintings published two years earlier was titled, of all things, Necronomicon. Alien is cosmic horror in a spacesuit. The crew of the Nostromo stumble onto something ancient and utterly alien, and the creature does not hate them. It simply uses them.

Think of John Carpenter's The Thing, from nineteen eighty-two, where a shapeshifting organism from the deep past turns a research station in Antarctica, the same frozen continent as At the Mountains of Madness, into a place where no one can trust what anyone else really is. Carpenter returned to the theme in In the Mouth of Madness, from nineteen ninety-four, in which a horror novelist's books begin to rewrite reality itself. It is, more or less openly, a film about what happens when a Lovecraft story escapes the page.

In the twenty-first century, the influence became more subtle. Jeff VanderMeer's novel Annihilation, adapted for film by Alex Garland in twenty eighteen, follows an expedition into a zone where nature has been quietly rewritten by something no one understands. There are no tentacles, no ancient gods. Just a slow, beautiful, terrifying sense that the rules have changed and that the change does not care about the people inside it. Richard Stanley's Colour Out of Space, starring Nicolas Cage, went back to a Lovecraft original and painted it in impossible, saturated colour.

And then there was the first season of True Detective, in twenty fourteen. On the surface, it is a crime drama about two detectives in Louisiana. Underneath, it is soaked in older weird fiction, especially Robert W. Chambers' The King in Yellow from eighteen ninety-five, a book Lovecraft himself admired, with its lost city of Carcosa. Its philosophical detective, Rust Cohle, speaks in long, bleak monologues about consciousness as a tragic mistake, and the show's creator acknowledged the influence of the horror writer and philosopher Thomas Ligotti. For many viewers, that was their first encounter with cosmic pessimism, delivered in a cheap motel room by a man drinking beer from a can.

Cosmic horror has thrived in comics too. The Japanese artist Junji Ito's Uzumaki, serialised at the end of the nineteen-nineties, is about a small town slowly consumed by an obsession with spirals. The spiral is not evil. It is not even alive, exactly. It is a pattern, and the pattern is winning. It is one of the purest expressions of Lovecraftian dread ever put on paper, and it does not contain a single tentacle.

The weird goes digital

If Lovecraft's monsters are hard to show on film, there is one medium where they feel strangely at home, and that is the video game.

Games can do something film cannot. They can make you complicit. They can let you choose to open the door, read the book, go further down. And they can play with the one thing every player relies on completely, their own perception.

In two thousand and two, a game called Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem gave its characters a sanity meter, and when it ran low, the game began to lie to the player. The screen would appear to turn off. The game would pretend that your save file had been deleted. The horror leaked out of the story and into the machine itself. Amnesia: The Dark Descent, from twenty ten, made looking at the monsters actively harmful, so that players learned to turn away, which is the most Lovecraftian instinct of all.

Bloodborne, released by the Japanese studio FromSoftware in twenty fifteen, begins as a gothic tale of werewolves and plague, and slowly reveals itself to be something else entirely. It has a statistic called Insight. The more Insight your character gains, the more of the world's true nature they can perceive, including vast, crawling things that were there all along, clinging to the buildings, invisible until you knew enough to see them. Knowledge, in Bloodborne, is both power and contamination. Lovecraft would have recognised it at once.

More recently, a quiet little game called Dredge, from twenty twenty-three, cast players as a fisherman in a remote archipelago. You catch fish, sell them, upgrade your boat. But some of the fish are wrong. Some have too many eyes. And at night, out on the water, it is best not to stay too long. It is cosmic horror at the scale of a fishing trip, and it found a huge audience.

The internet, meanwhile, built a cosmic horror tradition of its own, and built it the way Lovecraft's circle did, collaboratively. The SCP Foundation began in two thousand and seven as a single post on an online forum, a clinical containment report about a strange statue. It grew into an enormous shared wiki of anomalous objects and entities, written as the dry internal documents of a secret organisation trying to keep the impossible locked away. Its most memorable entries are pure cosmic horror, catalogued in the language of bureaucracy. The Backrooms, which began as a single eerie photograph posted online in twenty nineteen, imagined an endless maze of empty yellow office rooms just behind the surface of reality. And a wave of so-called analogue horror, low-budget web series made to look like old broadcast television and emergency alerts, found dread in static, test patterns and calm instructions not to look at the sky.

Even this medium, the podcast, has played its part. The Magnus Archives, which ran from twenty sixteen to twenty twenty-one, told a vast cosmic story through recorded statements read aloud in an archive, and Welcome to Night Vale turned eldritch strangeness into the cheerful news bulletins of a small desert town. Horror, it turns out, works very well when it is whispered directly into your ear.

Why cosmic horror now

So why has this particular kind of fear flourished in our time, more than in Lovecraft's own?

Part of the answer lies in philosophy. Thomas Ligotti, whose short stories began appearing in the nineteen-eighties, pushed Lovecraft's cosmicism into something even bleaker and stranger, and in twenty ten published a book-length argument that human consciousness itself is a kind of horror. The philosopher Eugene Thacker, in a book called In the Dust of This Planet, argued that horror fiction is one of the few places where our culture tries to think about a world without us in it. And the late critic Mark Fisher, in The Weird and the Eerie, drew a careful line between two feelings. The weird, he suggested, is the sense that something is present that does not belong. The eerie is the sense that something is absent that should be there, or that something is acting when nothing should be. Both, he argued, are ways of glimpsing the outside, the vast reality beyond our comfortable human frame.

But part of the answer is simpler, and closer to home. Lovecraft's monsters were metaphors for scale, for forces so large and so old that a single human life is meaningless beside them. In his time, that was a philosophical position. In ours, it is often simply the news. We live with systems too large for any one person to understand, a changing climate measured in centuries, financial markets that move faster than thought, networks and algorithms that shape our lives according to logic none of us can see. None of these things hate us. They do not love us either. They simply proceed, vast and indifferent, while we try to make sense of them from the inside.

Cosmic horror gives that feeling a shape. It says, yes, the world may be larger and stranger and less concerned with you than you were raised to believe. And then, at its best, it asks the next question. What do you do with that knowledge? Lovecraft's narrators went mad. But the writers who answered him, LaValle and Ruff and Emrys and Jemisin and many others, suggest a different response. You find the other people standing at the edge of the abyss with you. You look at each other instead of into the dark. And you hold on.

I am Providence

Lovecraft was buried in Swan Point Cemetery in Providence, in his family's plot. For forty years, his name appeared only on the family monument. In nineteen seventy-seven, his readers raised the money for a headstone of his own. On it they carved a phrase from one of his letters, three words that are now visited by pilgrims from all over the world.

I am Providence.

It is a strange epitaph for a man who believed that nothing human would last, that the stars were cold and the gods were blind and every city would one day be dust. People leave things on that stone. Coins, pens, small carved tentacles, notes folded into squares. They come to pay respects to a man who would almost certainly have been uncomfortable with many of them.

And perhaps that is his real legacy. Not the monsters, or the forbidden books, or the unspeakable adjectives. But the question at the centre of his work, which turned out to be bigger than he was, and which every generation since has had to answer for itself. What does it mean to be small, in a universe that does not notice us?

He thought the answer was terror. A century of readers, writers and dreamers have been quietly suggesting that it might also be wonder. And company.
